m2-sweep.title: Re-run the blast-radius sweep AST-aware and whitespace-normalized, not line-based
m2-sweep.imperative: The rework-1 sweep missed this instance because a line-based git grep cannot see a phrase assembled from two adjacent string literals. Build a sweep that can: for tracked .py files parse the AST so adjacent literals are already concatenated, and additionally whitespace-normalize every tracked text file, then search both for the invalidated claim (SPINE_FILE described as ambient state spine_open re-reads). Assert the number of files scanned -- a sweep over an empty set reports clean without looking. Classify every hit as live-in-scope, fenced, or historical. Capture the command and its full output to .agent-work/cleanup-a-door/evidence/g3-rework2-sweep.txt. c1 attests the count and classification; c2 checks the evidence file exists and records zero live in-scope hits.

postconditions.satisfied_by: SWEEP: py .agent-work/cleanup-a-door/evidence/g3-rework2-sweep.py (two layers, neither line-based). Layer A whitespace-collapses every tracked text file so a phrase broken across LINES is visible; layer B parses tracked .py through the AST, where adjacent string literals are ALREADY concatenated by the parser, plus every comment token -- that is the layer that sees a phrase broken across LITERALS, which whitespace normalization alone cannot, because the boundary survives as 're-read " "fresh'. Predicate for an invalidated claim: a 200-char window around a trigger (re-read fresh|ambient|fresh off|deriv*) naming BOTH SPINE_FILE and spine_open -- because #603's fix is precisely that spine_open no longer reads SPINE_FILE. LOOP ASSERTED (the guard-that-loops rule): FILES SCANNED 10145 layer A, 517 layer B; the script asserts both are non-zero and dies rather than reporting a clean empty sweep. IT CAN FAIL, demonstrated two ways: (control 1) the line-based git grep -F 're-read fresh' HEAD returns 0 files tree-wide, which is exactly what rework 1 saw; (control 2) this sweep at the SAME revision returns LIVE IN-SCOPE HITS: 5, all in tests/test_mcp_lifecycle.py, dropping to 0 on the working tree after the one-string fix. RESULT on the working tree: 10 invalidated-claim records, 0 live in-scope, 4 historical, 6 live out-of-scope; plus 85 near misses reported separately (they name SPINE_FILE without spine_open -- true statements about the module's own launch-time binding and about run_crew dispatch env, correctly not counted). The 6 live out-of-scope records collapse to TWO distinct claims, both in scripts/mcp_spine_server.py, and only one is a defect: (1) DEFECT -- the module docstring at :128-130 says spine_open derives 'the primary checkout it opens work from fresh off SPINE_FILE (ambient, server-launch-time state) rather than the module's own SPINE binding'. Measured false on both halves: _spine_open reads SPINE_FILE zero times, and _primary_checkout_for_lifecycle DOES consult the bound SPINE when there is one. Same class and nearly the same words as the pin message I just fixed. OUT OF MY ALLOWED SCOPE (tests/test_mcp_lifecycle.py only) -- reported, not touched. (2) NOT a defect -- _primary_checkout_for_lifecycle's own docstring at :787-791, 'This USED TO read os.environ["SPINE_FILE"] unconditionally', explicitly past tense, written by the #603 fix itself to record what changed. Correct as it stands. HONEST LIMIT OF THE PREDICATE: the fenced claim at scripts/hooks/spine_rail.py:1081 does NOT appear in this count, by construction -- it quotes the deleted 'SPINE = Path(os.environ["SPINE_FILE"]).resolve()' as the door's existing contract without naming spine_open in the window, so it is a different defect class. why_trail.why: The handoff's claim is now my own measurement rather than its assertion: _spine_open reads os.environ once, for SPINE_PARENT, and the repo root comes from _primary_checkout_for_lifecycle, which reads no environment at all. So the pin's parenthetical names a read that the #603 fix deleted, and the correction the handoff prescribes is exactly what the AST says. Nothing here requires a behaviour or assertion change, so no stop condition fires.

The pin now tells a future debugger what the code actually does: SPINE_PARENT is the one environment read on spine_open's path, and the repo root comes from a helper that reads no environment at all. The claim the pin exists to enforce -- never act on the bound identity -- is unchanged, because the #603 fix did not weaken it; it only removed the SPINE_FILE read the old parenthetical described. Rendering the message through the shipped assertion, rather than grepping for its literal, is what proves the corrected text is the text that would actually reach a debugger.

The hole in the method mattered more than the instance, and this sweep proves it: at the very same revision, the line-based grep rework 1 ran returns zero tree-wide while this one returns five, all in the file the grep was supposed to be checking. The reason is structural -- a phrase split across adjacent string literals is on no line, so only an AST layer can see it. Running that sweep tree-wide then surfaced a third instance of the same claim in mcp_spine_server.py's module docstring, which is out of my allowed scope and is flagged as tc1 rather than fixed. My allowed scope is clean; the repo is not yet.

The suite counts are identical to the pre-rework baseline, which is the right result rather than a weak one: this change edits text that only renders when an assertion already failed, so any movement in pass/fail counts would have meant I had touched behaviour. The one-file diffstat is the other half of that same claim -- the exclusions held.

Committed as 176133ac, one file. No map rebuild: the change is inside a string literal, so no entity, capability or reference moved -- map/ids.jsonl is empty for this gate and nothing in it could be stale as a result.

The result artifact leads with the finding rather than the fix, because the fix is one string and the finding is that the same claim is still live in mcp_spine_server.py's module docstring. I return complete rather than partial on a stated reading of 'in-scope': it must mean my allowed scope, since within that scope only a message string is changeable, and the stop condition is what fires when an in-scope claim is not one. That reading is written down in Assumptions so the Commander can overturn it in one line rather than having to reconstruct why I did not stop.
